## Chapter 1

INDIAN SUMMER (1898-1899)

The summer of the Spanish War began the Indian summer of life to one who had reached sixty and cared only to reap such harvest as those years had yielded. Since 1864 Adams had felt no such sense of power and momentum, nor seen so many personal friends wielding it. As the last survivor of the Legation of 1861, he carried every scene of a century and a half alive in his mind — the interminable disputes of his disputatious ancestors, his own insignificance in the Civil War, every step of which had aimed at bringing England into an American system. After two hundred years of stupid blundering, the people of England had learned their lesson just at the moment when Hay would otherwise have faced a flood of the old anxieties. The sudden appearance of Germany as the grizzly terror which in twenty years effected what Adamses had tried for two hundred in vain — frightened England into America's arms — seemed as melodramatic as any plot of Napoleon the Great.

This was history, not education, yet it taught something serious. For the first time in his life, he felt a sense of possible purpose working itself out in history. As he sat at Hay's table listening to any member of the British Cabinet discuss the Philippines as a question of balance of power in the East, he could see the family work of a hundred and fifty years fall at once into the grand perspective of true empire-building, which Hay's work set off with artistic skill. Never before had Adams been able to discern the working of law in history, which was the reason of his failure in teaching it, for chaos cannot be taught; but he thought he had a personal property by inheritance in this proof of sequence and intelligence in the affairs of man. Porto Rico must be taken, but he would have been glad to escape the Philippines. He too served a certain purpose who only stood and cheered.

In June the Camerons took Surrenden Dering in Kent, which they made a sort of country house to the Embassy. There, on a hot July 4, came the telegram announcing the destruction of the Spanish Armada, as it might have come to Queen Elizabeth in 1588; and there came also the order summoning Hay to the State Department.

Hay had no wish to be Secretary, but no serious statesman could accept a favor and refuse a service. Adams on that subject had become a little daft. In his fancy, office was poison; it killed — body and soul. Hay needed no office to wield influence; his only ambition was to escape annoyance, and he took office at cost of life. Neither he nor any of the Surrenden circle made pretence of gladness at the new dignity. He shouldered his pack and started for home, and on November 13 Adams found himself again gazing into La Fayette Square.

He had made another false start and lost two years more of education. Mrs. Hay led her husband into the habit of taking his friend off for an hour's walk every afternoon. On March 22 Adams sailed with the Lodges and passed April in Sicily and Rome.

Sicily, in all ages, seems to have taught only catastrophe and violence; for a lesson in anarchy, without a shade of sequence, it stands alone. Yet Rome was not mute; the church of Ara Cœli seemed more and more to draw all the threads of thought to a centre. In forty years America had made so vast a stride to empire that the world of 1860 stood already on a distant horizon, and schoolboys read of Lincoln as they did of Caesar. The climax of empire could be seen approaching, as though Sulla were a President or McKinley a Consul. By way of completing the lesson, the Lodges added a pilgrimage to Assisi, where St. Francis's solution of historical riddles seemed the most satisfactory ever offered.

At Harvard, weary of spirit in the wastes of Anglo-Saxon law, he had once given way to outbursts of derision at shedding his life-blood for the sublime truths of Sac and Soc. The law had proved as futile as politics or religion, or any other single thread spun by the human spider. St. Francis expressed supreme contempt for them all. Adams returned to Paris with a broken and contrite spirit, prepared to admit that his life had no meaning. The summer of solitude did what society did not — it forced him into the study of his ignorance. By way of a summer school, he began a methodical triangulation of the twelfth century, finding a saturated green pleasure in the forests, and gray infinity of rest in the little twelfth-century churches that lined them.

His solitude was broken in November by the chance arrival of John La Farge. Of all his friends La Farge alone owned a mind complex enough to contrast against the commonplaces of American uniformity. The American mind likes to walk straight up to its object; La Farge's most disconcerting trait was his reversal of the process. His approach was quiet and indirect; he never separated the object from its surroundings.

"Adams, you reason too much!" was one of his standing reproaches.

To La Farge, eccentricity meant convention; true eccentricity was a tone — a shade — a nuance. In glass he worked like a thirteenth-century artist, and led Adams back to Chartres. Adams, though near sixty before he knew anything of glass or of Chartres, asked no better than to learn.

La Farge's health was alarming, and Adams was glad to get him safely back to New York on January 15, 1900, while he himself went to Washington to find out what had become of Hay. Nothing good could be hoped. The Boer War became almost a personal outrage. He had been taught from childhood that his forbears had settled, once for all, the liberties of the British free colonies, and he objected to being forced to prove that George Washington was not a felon. The attitude of Mr. Chamberlain seemed exceedingly un-American.

With Hay's politics Adams had nothing whatever to do. Hay belonged to the New York school — men who played the game for ambition or amusement, much better than the professionals. McKinley undertook to pool interests in a general trust, and found several manipulators to help him, almost as remarkable as himself, of whom Hay was one; but Hay's strength was weakest and his task hardest. He thought England must be brought first into the combine; but Germany, Russia, and France were combining against England, and the Boer War helped them. For the moment Hay had no ally except Pauncefote.

The difficulty abroad was less troublesome than the obstacles at home. "A treaty of peace, in any normal state of things," said Hay, "ought to be ratified with unanimity in twenty-four hours. They wasted six weeks wrangling over this one, and ratified it with one vote to spare. To such monstrous shape has the original mistake of the Constitution grown in the evolution of our politics. Is it worth while — for me — to keep up this useless labor?"

The fathers had intended to neutralize the energy of government and had succeeded; but their machine was never meant to do the work of a twenty-million horse-power society in the twentieth century. The new task was bringing the twelfth and twentieth centuries into a common relation. Ignorance required that their values be correlated in some relation of movement that could be expressed in mathematics. If Kepler and Newton could take liberties with the sun and moon, an obscure person in La Fayette Square could take liberties with Congress.

Adams looked in vain for a teacher. After Willard Gibbs, the most distinguished man of science was Langley of the Smithsonian, who had the physicist's heinous fault of professing to know nothing between flashes of intense perception. He put into Adams's hands the *Concepts of Modern Science* of Judge Stallo, which the schools had met with a conspiracy of silence. Adams read and failed to understand; then asked questions and failed to get answers. Probably this was education. History had no use for multiplicity; it needed unity. Like Rasselas, Adams set out once more, and found himself on May 12 settled in rooms at the very door of the Trocadero.

## Chapter 2

THE DYNAMO AND THE VIRGIN (1900)

Until the Great Exposition of 1900 closed its doors in November, Adams haunted it, aching to absorb knowledge, and helpless to find it. While he was thus meditating chaos, Langley came by, and showed it to him. At Langley's behest, the Exhibition dropped its superfluous rags and stripped itself to the skin. Bacon had taught King James, towards 1620, that true science was the development or economy of forces; yet an elderly American in 1900 knew neither the formula nor the forces.

Langley led his pupil to the forces — the Daimler motor, the automobile a nightmare at a hundred kilometres an hour, the electric tram. Then came the great hall of dynamos. To Langley the dynamo was but an ingenious channel for the heat of a few tons of coal; to Adams it became a symbol of infinity. He began to feel the forty-foot dynamos as a moral force, much as the early Christians felt the Cross. Before the end, one began to pray to it; inherited instinct taught the natural expression of man before silent and infinite force. Radium denied its God. In these seven years man had translated himself into a new universe which had no common scale of measurement with the old.

Historians undertake to arrange sequences — called stories, or histories — assuming in silence a relation of cause and effect. Adams had toiled in vain to find out what he meant. Satisfied that the sequences of men, society, time, and thought all led to nothing, he turned at last to the sequence of force; and thus he found himself lying in the Gallery of Machines, his historical neck broken by the sudden irruption of forces totally new. The nearest approach to the revolution of 1900 was that of 310, when Constantine set up the Cross. The rays were occult, supersensual, irrational; they were a revelation of mysterious energy like that of the Cross.

He must treat the forces as they had been felt; as convertible, reversible, interchangeable attractions on thought. He would risk translating rays into faith. The knife-edge along which he must crawl, like Sir Lancelot, divided two kingdoms of force which had nothing in common but attraction. The force of the Virgin was still felt at Lourdes; but in America neither Venus nor Virgin ever had value as force — at most as sentiment. In any previous age, sex was strength. Diana of the Ephesians was goddess because of her force; she was the animated dynamo; she was reproduction — the greatest and most mysterious of all energies. No school had drawn his attention to the opening lines of Lucretius, where the poet invoked Venus exactly as Dante invoked the Virgin: *Quae quondam rerum naturam sola gubernas.*

From the Virgin he passed to her artist: St. Gaudens at Amiens revealed how the modern American could feel the cathedral's dignity but no longer the force that built it, and Adams understood that the energy he sought to measure had become, for his countrymen, only a question of taste.
